title: Set a wind-up metronome to 60 beats per minute: slide the weight to the 60 mark, then start the pendulum swinging
instruction: Set the metronome to 60 beats per minute and start it ticking.
context: Setting a mechanical metronome before practising is a routine act for music students and teachers. The tempo is set by sliding a small weight along the pendulum rod to a line on the scale behind it. The rod is notched at every mark and the weight's sprung tooth clicks from notch to notch, so it takes a firm push along the rod (about 3 N), and near 60 the notches are only 1 to 2 mm apart. The pendulum also swings freely, so a push across the rod swings it instead of moving the weight. Then the pendulum has to be swung to one side and let go cleanly, without knocking it or the metronome.
setup: World frame: x forward from the arms, y to the left. One fixed layout. Metronome: a mechanical wind-up pyramid metronome with a Maelzel scale from 40 to 208 (for example the Wittner Maelzel 800 series). It has a wooden case 22.5 cm tall on a 123 x 134 mm plinth (front to back x side to side) and weighs 500 g in total. Its front cover is removed and set aside off the table, the bell is switched off and the spring is fully wound. It stands on the bare table on the centre line between the arms, with the centre of its base 33 cm forward of the arm bases and its scale facing the arms. Its base is outlined in tape on the table. Pendulum: a flat steel rod (4 x 0.8 mm) that pivots 7.5 cm above the table, about 3 cm behind the case's front edge, and runs from 4.5 cm below the pivot to 15 cm above it. A 70 g brass weight is fixed 4 cm below the pivot, inside the case. The brass sliding weight (20 g; 22 mm wide, 18 mm tall and 12 mm deep, in front of the rod) is held on the rod by a spring clip whose tooth sits in a notch. The rod is notched at every scale mark, and pushing the weight along the rod with about 3 N clicks it into the next notch. The scale plate stands 4.5 mm behind the rod. One 0.6 mm line per Maelzel mark (40, 42, ..., 58, 60, 63, ..., 208) runs to the right of the rod, and 40, 60, 80, 100, 120, 160 and 208 are numbered. The tempo is read at the weight's top edge. In the simulation the lines lie 35.2 mm (208) to 126.4 mm (40) above the pivot. The 58, 60 and 63 lines (and notches) are at 117.6, 116.5 and 114.9 mm. Start: the pendulum is out of its storage holder and stands at rest, upright at the centre, and the weight's top edge is on the 120 line. Nothing else is on the table. Screenshot: left, the top camera (the scale faces the arms, toward the bottom of the image); right, the left wrist camera's view of the untouched metronome a moment later, with the weight on the 120 line and the numbered scale to the right of the rod. Estimates: the pendulum's masses (70 g fixed weight, 20 g sliding weight, the rod) and the clip's 3 N click. A real metronome's own printed scale sets where 60 is.
scoring: Scored at the end of the trial from video: a phone on a stand in front, level with the 60 line (so the weight's top edge is read without parallax), and a second phone above for the hands' clearance. The episode ends once the score has been 1.0 for 1 s. 'Ticking on its own' means that over the last 5 s, no part of either robot hand or wrist came within 5 cm of the metronome. In those 5 s the pendulum passed the centre line at least four times, and every swing between two of those passes reached at least 15 degrees from upright to each side, measured on the video frame at the swing's end against the case's centre line. 'At 60' means the weight is clicked into the 60 notch, with its top edge on the 60 line (in simulation: the 60 line is the line nearest its top edge). 'Near 60' means it is in a notch from 52 to 69. 1.0: at 60 and ticking on its own, at 56 to 64 beats per minute, timed from the first to the last centre pass in those 5 s (for example four consecutive passes, three beats, 2.81 to 3.21 s apart). 0.75: ticking on its own with the weight near 60, but not scoring 1.0. 0.5: at 60 but not ticking on its own (still, swinging under 15 degrees, or a hand within 5 cm). 0.25: ticking on its own with the weight elsewhere, or the weight near 60 but not ticking on its own. 0: anything else. Also 0 whenever the case is tilted more than 5 degrees, its base has slid more than 2 cm out of its outline, or it has turned more than 10 degrees. The score stays 0 for the rest of the trial once the case has tilted past 20 degrees (tipped over or lifted). In simulation every condition is checked at each control step, and the hands and wrists are the vertices of their collision hulls. The metronome there is its case's bounding box, the rod and the sliding weight.
reset_notes: Before each trial: wind the spring fully (a full wind runs the metronome for several minutes), stop the pendulum upright, slide the weight back so that its top edge is on the 120 line, and put the case back in its tape outline, square to the arms.
fidelity: Rigid parts at real size. The tempo comes from gravity on the jointed pendulum (frictionless pivot, rod, both weights); the scale lines sit where it ticks with a 25 degree swing. The rod is notched at every mark by contact geometry (30 degree flanks); a sprung tooth on the weight clicks into the notches (about 3 N to move it, estimate). No escapement: the pendulum swings freely and slowly loses swing, staying over 15 degrees for the scored 5 s. No tick sound.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0.0 (reached toward the metronome but neither set nor started it; 1,600-step limit). Scripted demo: 1.0 (full score from step 651; success ended the episode at step 670, 33.5 s).
